claim: The vestibular system detects head motion in space via five peripheral sensory organs located bilaterally in the inner ears: the three semicircular canals and the two otolith organs.
source: The vestibular system detects head motion in space via five peripheral sensory organs located bilaterally in the inner ears: the three semicircular canals, which sense angular rotation in three orthogonal axes, and the two otolith organs, which detect linear acceleration (translational acceleration and gravity) in both horizontal and vertical planes (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, representing established anatomical knowledge of the vestibular system.

claim: The three semicircular canals sense angular rotation in three orthogonal axes.
source: The vestibular system detects head motion in space via five peripheral sensory organs located bilaterally in the inner ears: the three semicircular canals, which sense angular rotation in three orthogonal axes, and the two otolith organs, which detect linear acceleration (translational acceleration and gravity) in both horizontal and vertical planes (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, representing established knowledge of vestibular anatomy and function.

claim: The two otolith organs detect linear acceleration (translational acceleration and gravity) in both horizontal and vertical planes.
source: The vestibular system detects head motion in space via five peripheral sensory organs located bilaterally in the inner ears: the three semicircular canals, which sense angular rotation in three orthogonal axes, and the two otolith organs, which detect linear acceleration (translational acceleration and gravity) in both horizontal and vertical planes (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, representing established knowledge of vestibular physiology.

claim: The brain uses vestibular information to ensure visual and postural stability, as well as an accurate and stable perception of self-motion and orientation during movement through space.
source: In turn, the brain uses vestibular information to ensure visual and postural stability, as well as an accurate and stable perception of our self-motion and orientation as we move through space (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, representing established knowledge of vestibular function.

claim: When vestibular sensors are damaged, essential functions are disrupted causing disabling symptoms including blurred vision, dizziness, unstable posture, and gait.
source: When the vestibular sensors are damaged, these essential functions are disrupted causing disabling symptoms—e.g., blurred vision, dizziness, unstable posture, and gait—which can reduce a patient's ability to participate in even the simplest of daily activities.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established clinical knowledge of vestibular dysfunction.

claim: More than 1.8 million adults worldwide suffer from bilateral loss of vestibular functions.
source: It is estimated that more than 1.8 million adults worldwide suffer from bilateral loss of vestibular functions (Boutros et al., 2019a; Schoo et al., 2024).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Plasticity occurs within the vestibular pathways following sensory loss.
source: While plasticity does occur within the vestibular pathways following sensory loss (Sadeghi et al., 2012) and can partially improve function (Nashner et al., 1982; Sprenger et al., 2017; Whitney et al., 2016), there had been no effective restorative treatment for those who could not compensate centrally (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Plasticity within vestibular pathways can partially improve function following sensory loss.
source: While plasticity does occur within the vestibular pathways following sensory loss (Sadeghi et al., 2012) and can partially improve function (Nashner et al., 1982; Sprenger et al., 2017; Whitney et al., 2016), there had been no effective restorative treatment for those who could not compensate centrally (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: There had been no effective restorative treatment for patients who could not compensate centrally for vestibular loss.
source: While plasticity does occur within the vestibular pathways following sensory loss (Sadeghi et al., 2012) and can partially improve function (Nashner et al., 1982; Sprenger et al., 2017; Whitney et al., 2016), there had been no effective restorative treatment for those who could not compensate centrally (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Vestibular prostheses detect head movements and convert them into VIII nerve stimulation, substituting for damaged peripheral sensors.
source: These devices detect head movements and convert them into VIII nerve stimulation, substituting for the damaged peripheral sensors.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, describing the basic mechanism of vestibular prostheses.

claim: At rest, primate vestibular afferents display a robust baseline firing rate of approximately 100 spikes/s in macaque monkeys.
source: At rest (e.g. when there is no head motion), primate vestibular afferents display a robust baseline firing rate (i.e. ~100 spikes/s in macaque monkeys; reviewed in Cullen, 2019; Figure 1B, left).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation to a review and illustrated in Figure 1B, representing established neurophysiological data.

claim: During head motion, the firing rate of a vestibular afferent is modulated relative to baseline rate depending on the deflection direction of the innervated hair cells.
source: During head motion, the firing rate of a given afferent is then modulated relative to this baseline rate depending on the deflection direction of the innervated hair cells (Figure 1B, middle and right).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B, representing established knowledge of vestibular afferent physiology.

claim: Each vestibular afferent conveys information about head movement in two opposite directions by either increasing or decreasing firing rate relative to its baseline.
source: As a result, each vestibular afferent conveys information about head movement in two opposite directions, by either increasing or decreasing firing rate relative to its baseline.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established knowledge of vestibular afferent encoding.

claim: The most common known cause of hair cell damage is toxicity from systemic aminoglycoside drugs such as gentamicin.
source: The most common known cause of hair cells damage is toxicity from systemic aminoglycoside drugs (e.g. gentamicin; Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Those with congenital deafness due to loss of auditory hair cells can also lack properly functioning vestibular hair cells.
source: In addition, those with congenital deafness due to loss of auditory hair cells can also lack properly functioning vestibular hair cells (Delmaghani and El-Amraoui, 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The organization of the three semicircular canals is orthogonal, allowing for comprehensive detection of angular head rotation along three distinct axes.
source: First, the organization of the three semicircular canals is orthogonal, an arrangement that allows for comprehensive detection of angular head rotation along three distinct axes (reviewed in Cullen, 2019; Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation to a review and illustrated in Figure 1A, representing established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Hair cells within each semicircular canal are aligned such that their polarity corresponds to the primary axis of maximum sensitivity.
source: Additionally, the hair cells within each semicircular canal are aligned such that their polarity corresponds to the primary axis of maximum sensitivity, ensuring optimal detection of angular head movements along each axis (reviewed in Goldberg et al., 2012; Figure 1A and B, red arrows).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation to a review and illustrated in Figures 1A and 1B, representing established knowledge of vestibular anatomy.

claim: Hair cells in each semicircular canal are innervated by a distinct nerve bundle.
source: Moreover, the hair cells in each canal are innervated by a distinct nerve bundle.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The orthogonal organization of semicircular canals allows for axis-specific electrical stimulation via targeted electrode placement within each of the three canals.
source: Taken together, this organization thus allows for axis-specific electrical stimulation via targeted electrode placement within each of the three semicircular canals.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing an inference from anatomical knowledge applied to prosthesis design.

claim: It is possible to transform 3D head motion into a canal-based reference frame by measuring head motion using a 3D gyroscope and projecting this motion into the three rotational axes of the canals.
source: Accordingly, it is possible to transform three-dimensional (3D) head motion into a canal-based reference frame by measuring head motion using a 3D gyroscope and then projecting this motion into the three rotational axes of the canals (Figure 2A; Boutros et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 2A, representing an engineering approach supported by published research.

claim: Results from both animal studies and clinical trials have demonstrated the ability to induce 3D reflexive eye movements aligned with the respective canal plane using vestibular prostheses.
source: Indeed, results from both animal studies and clinical trials have demonstrated the ability to induce 3D reflexive eye movements aligned with the respective canal plane using this approach (Figure 2C; Boutros et al., 2019a; Dai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 2C, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: Small misalignments in prosthesis-evoked eye movements generally display significant improvement within the first week of continuous stimulation due to adaptation within central vestibular pathways.
source: Due to current spread between electrodes, these responses initially show some misalignment. Fortunately, these small misalignments generally display significant improvement within the first week of continuous stimulation due to adaptation within central vestibular pathways (Dai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The brain adapted to misaligned prosthetic stimulation (where one canal plane was deliberately translated into stimulation of a different canal afferent) resulting in accurate eye movements within 2 weeks.
source: Moreover, the brain's remarkable adaptability to misaligned prosthetic input was directly exemplified in a study by Lewis et al., 2003, where electrical stimulation of one canal plane was deliberately translated into stimulation of a different canal afferent. Despite this discrepancy, the brain adapted to the misaligned stimulation, resulting in accurate eye movements within 2 weeks.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The human vestibulo-ocular reflex can adapt to extreme misalignment (180 degrees) following continuous wearing of reversing prisms.
source: Overall, these impressive results are not surprising, as it is well known that the human vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) can adapt to extreme misalignment (180 degrees) following continuous wearing of reversing prisms (Gonshor and Jones, 1976).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Vestibular prostheses are typically only implanted in one ear to minimize potential risks and costs compared to bilateral implantation in ongoing clinical trials.
source: In ongoing clinical trials, vestibular prostheses are typically only implanted in one ear to minimize the potential risks and costs as compared to bilateral implantation (e.g. Boutros et al., 2019a; Golub et al., 2014; Guinand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Bidirectional sensitivity in vestibular prostheses has been achieved by modulating stimulation rates about a baseline rate of typically 100-150 pulses/s.
source: For example, bidirectional sensitivity has been achieved by modulating the stimulation rates about a baseline rate of typically ~100–150 pulses/s (e.g. Boutros et al., 2019a; Dai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Implanted patients and animals must adapt to applied baseline stimulation prior to receiving head motion-dependent modulation (approximately 30 min in patients, 3 hr in rhesus monkeys, and <1 day in squirrel monkeys and guinea pigs).
source: Implanted patients and animals thus must first adapt to this applied baseline stimulation prior to receiving head motion-dependent modulation (approximately 30 min in patients [Boutros et al., 2019a], 3 hr in rhesus monkeys [Dai et al., 2013], and <1 day in squirrel monkeys and guinea pigs [Merfeld et al., 2006; Merfeld et al., 2007]).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Regular afferents fire action potentials at regular intervals at rest while irregular afferents fire with irregular intervals.
source: Most notably, as their names suggest, regular afferents fire action potentials at regular intervals at rest while irregular afferents do so with irregular intervals (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3A, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: Irregular afferents respond more readily to electrical stimulation than regular afferents and could be preferentially recruited in response to prosthetic stimulation.
source: In the context of vestibular prosthesis development, it is especially noteworthy that irregular afferents respond more readily to electrical stimulation than regular afferents and thus could be preferentially recruited in response to prosthetic stimulation (Goldberg et al., 1984; Minor and Goldberg, 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: At relatively high electrical currents typically used for vestibular prostheses stimulation, both regular and irregular afferent types are thought to be recruited.
source: However, at the relatively high electrical currents typically used for vestibular prostheses stimulation, both afferent types are thought to be recruited (Mitchell et al., 2016; Steinhardt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Both regular and irregular canal afferents display high-pass tuning in their responses to head rotation, with response gains and phase leads increasing with increasing stimulus frequency.
source: Both regular and irregular afferents display high-pass tuning in their responses to head rotation; their response gains and phase leads increase with increasing stimulus frequency (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: Irregular afferents show stronger high-pass tuning than regular afferents.
source: Moreover, irregular afferents show stronger high-pass tuning than their regular counterparts.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: Irregular afferent response gains are greater than those of regular afferents over much of the physiologically relevant range of head motion.
source: Notably, irregular afferent response gains are greater than those of regular afferents over much of the physiologically relevant range of head motion (Figure 3B, top).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: The responses of irregular afferents reach higher phase leads with increasing frequency such that they actually encode angular head acceleration (rather than velocity) at higher frequencies.
source: In addition, the responses of irregular afferents reach higher phase leads with increasing frequency such that they actually encode angular head acceleration (rather than velocity) at higher frequencies (Figure 3B, bottom).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: The high-pass tuning displayed by regular and irregular afferents is well described by linear models at low frequencies and amplitudes of motion.
source: Overall, the high-pass tuning displayed by regular and irregular afferents is well described by linear models at low frequencies and amplitudes of motion (reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Vestibular stimuli experienced during natural behaviors often exceed both the amplitude and frequency range used in standard laboratory experiments in both humans and animal models.
source: A major finding within the last decade is that vestibular stimuli experienced during natural behaviors often exceed both the amplitude and frequency range used in standard laboratory experiments in both humans and animal models (Carriot et al., 2014; Carriot et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Natural stimuli will easily drive the firing of vestibular afferents into cut-off and/or saturation such that they exhibit substantial nonlinearities.
source: Importantly, such natural stimuli will easily drive the firing of vestibular afferents into cut-off and/or saturation such that they exhibit substantial nonlinearities (Figure 4A and B; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figures 4A and 4B, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: Linear models are not able to describe the responses of vestibular afferents across natural behaviors.
source: Accordingly, linear models are not able to describe the responses of afferents across natural behaviors.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing an inference from experimental findings.

claim: A linear-nonlinear cascade model including a nonlinearity well approximated by a sigmoidal function is required to faithfully represent vestibular afferent responses.
source: Instead, a linear-nonlinear cascade model (Figure 4C)—including a nonlinearity that is well approximated by a sigmoidal function—is required to faithfully represent vestibular afferent responses (Mackrous et al., 2022; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 4C, representing experimental findings from published research.

claim: Conventional vestibular prosthesis mappings directly link instantaneous head velocity to a specific stimulation rate with constant gain and no phase lead at all frequencies.
source: Generally, these mappings have been programmed to directly link angular head velocity to a specific stimulation rate in the encoding scheme (i.e. constant gain and no phase lead at all frequencies; Figure 5, top; see Boutros et al., 2019a; Chow et al., 2021; Perez Fornos et al., 2014, for examples)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 5, representing published prosthesis design approaches.

claim: Prior vestibular prosthesis mappings did not account for response dynamics of afferents over much of the frequency range corresponding to natural head motion (up to 20 Hz).
source: However, these mappings did not account for response dynamics of afferents over much of the frequency range corresponding to natural head motion (i.e. up to 20 Hz; Carriot et al., 2014, Carriot et al., 2017; reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The complete linear transfer functions of afferent coding were recently implemented into a vestibular prosthesis design.
source: While the nonlinearity is accounted for in all prosthesis mappings (e.g. Boutros et al., 2019a; Perez Fornos et al., 2014), only recently was the complete linear transfer functions of afferent coding implemented into a vestibular prosthesis design (Figure 5, bottom; Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 5, representing recent experimental work.

claim: There are three ongoing clinical trials focused on evaluating the potential of vestibular implants as a restorative treatment option for patients with vestibular loss.
source: At this time, there are three ongoing clinical trials focused on evaluating the potential of vestibular implants as a restorative treatment option for patients with such vestibular loss (i.e. University of Geneva and Maastricht University Hospital group [Crétallaz et al., 2020; Perez Fornos et al., 2014; Guinand et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016; Starkov et al., 2020], Johns Hopkins University group [Boutros et al., 2019a; Chow et al., 2021], and the University of Washington group [Phillips et al., 2013; Phillips et al., 2015; Rubinstein et al., 2020]).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Vestibular implants help relieve dizziness, reduce visual and postural instability, and improve quality of life in patients with vestibular sensory loss.
source: While these implants help relieve dizziness, reduce visual and postural instability, and improve quality of life in patients with vestibular sensory loss, it is important to emphasize that these essential vestibular functions remain only partially restored (see for example Chow et al., 2021).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Essential vestibular functions remain only partially restored by current vestibular implants.
source: While these implants help relieve dizziness, reduce visual and postural instability, and improve quality of life in patients with vestibular sensory loss, it is important to emphasize that these essential vestibular functions remain only partially restored (see for example Chow et al., 2021).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: VOR neurons receive direct VIII nerve input and project directly to extraocular motor neurons that control the eye muscles, constituting a very fast reflex pathway with approximately 5 ms latency.
source: VOR neurons receive direct VIII nerve input and in turn project directly to extraocular motor neurons that control the eye muscles, constituting a very fast reflex pathway (~5 ms latency; Huterer and Cullen, 2002).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: VOR neurons both respond to vestibular stimulation and are sensitive to eye movements, consistent with their role in gaze stabilization.
source: These neurons both respond to vestibular stimulation and are sensitive to eye movements, consistent with their role in gaze stabilization.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: VOR neurons receive their primary input from regular afferents.
source: Although VOR neurons receive direct projections from both afferent types, their primary input is from regular afferents (Boyle et al., 1992; Goldberg et al., 1987; Highstein et al., 1987; Minor and Goldberg, 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The response dynamics of regular afferents are well matched to compensate for delays within the VOR pathways and the dynamics of the oculomotor plant to produce VOR eye movements that temporally match the time course of head movement.
source: Overall, the response dynamics of regular afferents are well matched to compensate for the delays within the VOR pathways (i.e. synaptic, neural, and muscle activation time) and the dynamics of the oculomotor plant to produce VOR eye movements that temporally match the time course of the head movement (Boyle et al., 1992; Goldberg et al., 1987; Minor and Goldberg, 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The spiking activities of regular afferents, and consequently VOR neurons, faithfully encode the detailed time course of head motion, a coding feature required for the generation of accurate compensatory VOR eye movements.
source: In addition, the spiking activities of regular afferents, and consequently VOR neurons, faithfully encode the detailed time course of head motion, a coding feature that is required for the generation of accurate compensatory VOR eye movements (Mackrous et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: VO neurons respond to vestibular stimulation but are completely insensitive to eye movements.
source: Their name reflects the fact that they respond to vestibular stimulation but are completely insensitive to eye movements.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: VO neurons serve a vital role in controlling postural stability via the vestibulo-spinal pathway.
source: VO neurons serve a vital role in controlling postural stability via the vestibulo-spinal pathway.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: VO neurons receive their primary input from irregular rather than regular afferents.
source: In contrast to VOR neurons, VO neurons receive their primary input from irregular rather than regular afferents (Boyle et al., 1992; Goldberg et al., 1987; Highstein et al., 1987).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The more dynamic responses of irregular afferents (larger gains and phase leads) are optimized to generate robust postural responses which must account for the larger inertia of the body relative to the eye.
source: The more dynamic responses of irregular afferents (i.e. larger gains and phase leads) are optimized to generate robust postural responses which must account for the larger inertia of the body relative to the eye (Minor and Goldberg, 1991; Peterson, 1998).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The majority of VO neurons do not faithfully encode the time course of head movements but instead optimize coding via temporal whitening.
source: Moreover, in contrast to VOR neurons, the majority of VO neurons do not faithfully encode the time course of head movements but instead optimize coding via temporal whitening—a property thought to contribute to ensuring postural control and perceptual stability during everyday activities (Mackrous et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: VO neurons make important contributions to ascending vestibular pathways that contribute to perception of self-motion and orientation.
source: Importantly, in addition to mediating the VSR, VO neurons also make important contributions to ascending vestibular pathways that contribute to perception of self-motion and orientation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6B, representing established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: Current vestibular prostheses deliver a single stimulation pulse with large current amplitude to recruit all afferents within the target semicircular canal.
source: While the VOR and VSR, as well as the vestibulo-thalamic pathways, receive differential input weighting from regular and irregular afferents, current vestibular prostheses deliver a single stimulation pulse (with large current amplitude) to recruit all afferents within the target semicircular canal.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing current prosthesis design approaches.

claim: Prosthetic stimulation is likely to evoke similar activation of both regular and irregular afferents during a specific head motion, unlike natural stimulation.
source: Consequently, prosthetic stimulation, unlike natural stimulation, is likely to evoke similar activation of both regular and irregular afferents during a specific head motion.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing an inference from prosthesis design and neurophysiology.

claim: The VOR gain of healthy humans is approximately 1.0, meaning there is a compensatory eye velocity equal to the head velocity and in the opposite direction.
source: In healthy humans, the gain of the rotational VOR is ~1.0, meaning there is a compensatory eye velocity equal to the head velocity and in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established knowledge of normal VOR function.

claim: The VOR gain shows significant improvements when the prosthesis modulation is on versus off.
source: In general, the VOR gain shows significant improvements when the prosthesis modulation is on vs. off (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7C, representing experimental data.

claim: Visual acuity during treadmill walking and head impulses improves when the prosthesis is turned on.
source: This is accompanied by improved visual acuity during treadmill walking and head impulses when the prosthesis is turned on Ayiotis et al., 2022; Guinand et al., 2016; Starkov et al., 2020.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Patients in both the Johns Hopkins and Geneva-Maastricht clinical trials have reported reduced or absent oscillopsia symptoms when the prosthesis is turned on.
source: Additionally, while oscillopsia is not directly correlated with VOR gain across unilateral vestibular loss, bilateral vestibular loss, and cerebellar patient populations (Palla et al., 2008; Geisinger et al., 2024; Morland et al., 1998; Grunfeld et al., 2000), patients in both the Johns Hopkins and Geneva-Maastricht clinical trials have reported reduced or absent oscillopsia symptoms when the prosthesis is turned on Ayiotis et al., 2024; Boutros et al., 2019a; Chow et al., 2021; van Stiphout et al., 2022.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The gains of prosthesis-evoked VOR eye movements are not fully compensatory (gain<1).
source: The gains of the evoked VOR eye movements are not fully compensatory (i.e. gain<1; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7C, representing experimental data.

claim: VOR gains typically range between approximately 0.2 and 0.6 across implanted nonhuman primates and patients, with considerable variability.
source: Notably, there is considerable variability across both implanted nonhuman primates (Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022) and patients (Boutros et al., 2019a), such that VOR gains typically range between ~0.2 and 0.6.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Congruent extra-vestibular signals (visual, tactile, proprioception) can augment prosthetic stimulation to improve the VOR gain.
source: Fortunately, congruent extra-vestibular signals (i.e. visual, tactile, proprioception) can augment prosthetic stimulation to improve the VOR gain.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing an inference from experimental findings.

claim: Recent work in nonhuman primates has demonstrated greater VOR gain (though still not fully compensatory) from prosthetic stimulation in conjunction with physical rotation compared to prosthetic stimulation alone.
source: For example, recent work in nonhuman primates has demonstrated greater VOR gain (though still not fully compensatory) from prosthetic stimulation in conjunction with physical rotation compared to prosthetic stimulation alone (Dai et al., 2012; Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The effect of combined prosthetic stimulation and physical rotation on VOR gain is supra-additive, such that the gain during the combined condition was more than the sum of the gains in each separate condition alone.
source: The effect is supra-additive, such that the gain during the combined condition was more than the sum of the gains in each separate condition alone.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing experimental findings.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the afferents evoked stereotyped postural reflexes in the neck and limbs, in addition to compensatory VOR eye movements.
source: A classic study by Suzuki and Cohen, 1964, demonstrated that electrical stimulation of the afferents evoked stereotyped postural reflexes in the neck and limbs, in addition to compensatory VOR eye movements.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Short pulse trains applied via vestibular prostheses evoke not only VOR eye movements but also head motion contralateral to the stimulated side in implanted monkeys.
source: Short pulse trains applied via the vestibular prostheses evokes not only VOR eye movements, but also head motion contralateral to the stimulated side in implanted monkeys (Mitchell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The amplitude of prosthesis-evoked compensatory head movement increases with stimulation current amplitude and pulse rate.
source: Notably, the amplitude of the evoked compensatory head movement increases with stimulation current amplitude and pulse rate (Mitchell et al., 2013), and the activation of the neck muscles driving these compensatory head movements has been measured via EMG in patients (Fornos et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Experiments in implanted monkeys have shown improvements in posture when stimulation is provided by a vestibular prosthesis encoding head motion via pulse rate modulation during gaze shifts.
source: Experiments in implanted monkeys have shown improvements in posture when stimulation is provided by a vestibular prosthesis encoding head motion via pulse rate modulation during gaze shifts (Figure 8A; Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 8A, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: In implanted patients, short pulse trains applied via vestibular prostheses to each semicircular canal can generate whole-body postural responses that are biased toward the stimulated canal's plane.
source: Moreover, in implanted patients, short pulse trains applied via the vestibular prostheses to each semicircular canal can generate whole-body postural responses that are biased toward the stimulated canal's plane (Figure 8B; Phillips et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 8B, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: Modulated vestibular prosthetic stimulation improves performance on tests that directly assess vestibular function (such as the modified Romberg) and more general tests of posture and balance (including the timed walk and timed up and go tests) in implanted patients.
source: Similarly, more recent studies in implanted patients have demonstrated that modulated vestibular prosthetic stimulation improves performance on both tests that directly assess vestibular function, such as the modified Romberg, and more general tests of posture and balance, including the timed walk and timed up and go tests (Figure 8C; Chow et al., 2021).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 8C, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: At the onset of baseline prosthetic stimulation, implanted patients initially experience vestibular percepts (feelings of being rotated about the axis associated with the stimulated canal) that markedly attenuate within minutes.
source: However, it has been reported that, at the onset of baseline prosthetic stimulation, implanted patients initially experience vestibular percepts (i.e. feelings of being rotated about the axis associated with the stimulated canal), that markedly attenuate within minutes (e.g. Boutros et al., 2019a; Crétallaz et al., 2020; Guinand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: In experiments where monkeys were trained to align a light bar with gravity during static or continuous roll tilt, when tilts were accompanied by consequent prosthetic stimulation, the monkeys' reports of earth vertical were biased toward the direction of the stimulated canal.
source: In these experiments, monkeys were trained to align a light bar with gravity (i.e. earth vertical), either during static or continuous roll tilt. In both cases, when tilts were accompanied by consequent prosthetic stimulation, the monkeys' reports of earth vertical were biased toward the direction of the stimulated canal (Karmali et al., 2021; Lewis et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Noninvasive activation of the vestibular afferents via galvanic vestibular stimulation can increase activity in vestibular-sensitive subcortical and cortical areas even following bilateral vestibular loss.
source: Furthermore, we anticipate that since noninvasive activation of the vestibular afferents via galvanic vestibular stimulation can increase activity in vestibular-sensitive subcortical and cortical areas even following bilateral vestibular loss (Helmchen et al., 2020; Ruehl et al., 2022; Stephan et al., 2005), future work is likely to demonstrate that vestibular prostheses likewise stimulate these areas and can in turn produce improvements in navigation and spatial memory.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: VOR gains do not always correlate with broader vestibular functions.
source: However, most studies rely on VOR gains as a performance metric, which, though integral to the development of vestibular prostheses, do not always correlate with broader vestibular functions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing an inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Prior studies have reported the uncoupling of VOR function from self-motion perception in trained dancers.
source: For instance, prior studies have reported the uncoupling of VOR function from self-motion perception in trained dancers (Nigmatullina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: VOR gains poorly predict oscillopsia and fall risk in patients with bilateral vestibular loss.
source: VOR gains also poorly predict oscillopsia (Grunfeld et al., 2000) and fall risk (Dobbels et al., 2020) in patients with bilateral vestibular loss.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Individuals with vestibular implants can exhibit significant improvements in balance and gait despite suboptimal VOR gains.
source: Furthermore, individuals with vestibular implants can exhibit significant improvements in balance and gait despite suboptimal VOR gains (Chow et al., 2021).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Chronic conditions such as diabetes worsen self-motion perception thresholds, postural stability, and fall risk over time.
source: However, evidence suggests chronic conditions, such as diabetes, worsen self-motion perception thresholds, postural stability, and fall risk over time (La Scaleia et al., 2024).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The onset of baseline stimulation initially induces an asymmetry in vestibular input between the left and right ears that is interpreted as a head movement, causing nystagmus and postural instability.
source: In clinical trials of vestibular prostheses, the onset of baseline stimulation initially induces an asymmetry in vestibular input between the left and right ears that is interpreted as a head movement, and thus causes nystagmus and postural instability (Boutros et al., 2019a; Chow et al., 2021; Lewis et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Patients adapt to unilateral baseline stimulation rate over a relatively rapid time course.
source: Patients then adapt to this unilateral baseline stimulation rate over a relatively rapid time course (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 9A, representing experimental data.

claim: It has generally been assumed that adaptation to asymmetric vestibular input is mediated by central pathways, notably the commissural vestibular pathways.
source: It has generally been assumed that adaptation to this asymmetric vestibular input is mediated by central pathways, notably the commissural vestibular pathways (Figure 9B, green; Chiang et al., 2011; Della Santina et al., 2007; Merfeld et al., 2006; Merfeld et al., 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 9B, representing a hypothesis from published research.

claim: Experiments in rats and mice suggest plasticity in commissural pathways along with cerebellar and cortical vestibular areas produces changes in functional connectivity within minutes to hours following unilateral vestibular loss.
source: Indeed, experiments in rats and mice suggest plasticity in commissural pathways along with cerebellar and cortical vestibular areas that produces changes in functional connectivity within minutes to hours following unilateral vestibular loss, a condition similar to the onset of baseline stimulation with a vestibular prosthesis, which induces asymmetry in the input to central vestibular pathways (Cirelli et al., 1996; Grosch et al., 2021; Kai et al., 2022; Kitahara et al., 1997; Zwergal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Recent studies exploring the effect of prosthetic stimulation on central pathways have established that adaptation to prosthetic stimulation is mediated earlier in the pathway, at the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse.
source: Importantly however, recent studies exploring the effect of prosthetic stimulation on central pathways have instead established that adaptation to prosthetic stimulation is mediated earlier in the pathway, at the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse (Figure 9B, red; Mitchell et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 9B, representing experimental findings from published research.

claim: Experiments in implanted monkeys have revealed that prosthetic baseline stimulation leads to rapid and marked (>50%) reduction in efficacy of the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse, which substantially reduces efficacy of central vestibular pathways within minutes after stimulation onset.
source: Specifically, experiments in implanted monkeys have revealed that prosthetic baseline stimulation actually leads to the rapid and marked (>50%) reduction in efficacy of the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse, which in turn substantially reduces efficacy of central vestibular pathways within minutes after stimulation onset (Figure 9C; Mitchell et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 9C, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: Maladaptive prosthesis-induced reduction in synaptic efficacy occurs at the level of afferent input to both VOR neurons and VO neurons.
source: This maladaptive prosthesis-induced reduction in synaptic efficacy occurs at the level of afferent input to both the vestibular nuclei neurons that generate the VOR (Mitchell et al., 2016) and those that control VSR (Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Rapid complementary plasticity within inhibitory commissural nuclei network contributes to lessen the maladaptive effect of stimulation, but only partially improves behavioral VOR and VSR performance.
source: Rapid complementary plasticity within inhibitory commissural nuclei network contributes to lessen this maladaptive effect of stimulation. However, this rapid plasticity only partially improves behavioral VOR and VSR performance (Mitchell et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Only a few minutes of baseline prosthetic stimulation causes reductions in both VOR and VSR behavioral responses that can persist for more than 8 hr in absence of head motion or further prosthetic stimulation.
source: Critically, only a few minutes of baseline prosthetic stimulation causes reductions in both VOR and VSR behavioral responses that can persist for more than 8 hr in absence of head motion or further prosthetic stimulation (Mitchell et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The maladaptive reduction in the efficacy of the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse is speculated to be a key reason why implanted patients show incomplete restoration of function.
source: Overall, we speculate that the maladaptive reduction in the efficacy of the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse is a key reason why implanted patients show incomplete restoration of function (Boutros et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text as speculation and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The spiking activity of stimulated afferents synchronizes with prosthetic-driven pulse trains because their action potentials are tightly linked to the applied pulses.
source: The spiking activity of stimulated afferents synchronizes with prosthetic-driven pulse trains because their action potentials are tightly linked to the applied pulses (Mitchell et al., 2016; Steinhardt et al., 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Prosthesis-induced synchrony contrasts with what is observed across afferent population responses to natural head movement stimuli.
source: Importantly, this synchrony contrasts with what is observed across afferent population responses to natural head movement stimuli (Dale and Cullen, 2013; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: In vitro studies have demonstrated that repeated pulsatile stimulation of vestibular afferents induces long-term depression at the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse.
source: In vitro studies have demonstrated that repeated pulsatile stimulation of vestibular afferents induces long-term depression at the afferent-vestibular nuclei synapse (McElvain et al., 2010), thereby providing a mechanism for this observed reduction in central pathway efficacy (Mitchell et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Cochlear implant stimulation induces artificial synchrony in the firing of auditory afferents.
source: Correspondingly, it has been established that cochlear implant stimulation induces artificial synchrony in the firing of auditory afferents (Babalian et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2010; Sachs et al., 1983; Wu et al., 2016) as well as their target neurons in the cochlear nucleus (Babalian et al., 2003).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The synchrony induced by cochlear implant stimulation reduces the efficacy of central auditory pathways over time.
source: Furthermore, as in the vestibular system, the synchrony induced by cochlear implant stimulation reduces the efficacy of central auditory pathways over time (Hu et al., 2010; Runge et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: High-frequency subthreshold stimulation has been used for cochlear implants as a strategy to reduce synchrony.
source: One general strategy that has been used for cochlear implants is high-frequency subthreshold stimulation. In this strategy, stimulation is delivered at a frequency well beyond that of the afferents' maximum firing rate, typically 5 kHz (e.g. Babalian et al., 2003; Litvak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: The goal of high-frequency subthreshold stimulation approaches is to exploit the afferents' fixed refractory period to produce more variability in response timing across afferents.
source: The goal of both approaches is to exploit the afferents' fixed refractory period to produce more variability in response timing across afferents.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing the rationale for a stimulation strategy.

claim: Improvements in auditory thresholds have been reported for delayed pseudomonophasic (DPM) stimulation characterized by a brief, high-amplitude cathodic phase followed by a long, low-amplitude anodic phase.
source: A second strategy that has been successful in improving the performance of cochlear implants is the use of altered pulse waveforms, most notably delayed pseudomonophasic (DPM) asymmetric stimulus pulses. In particular, improvements in auditory thresholds have been reported for DPM stimulation characterized by a brief, high-amplitude cathodic phase followed by a long, low-amplitude anodic phase (Quass et al., 2020; van Wieringen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Hair cells provide both neurotrophic support and excitatory inputs to afferents.
source: However, neurophysiological studies of the auditory system have shown that hair cells provide both neurotrophic support and excitatory inputs to afferents.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing established knowledge from auditory system research.

claim: The loss of auditory hair cells significantly reduces the sensitivity of afferent fibers.
source: Accordingly, the loss of auditory hair cells not only significantly reduces the sensitivity of afferents fibers (e.g. Hartmann et al., 1984; Kiang and Moxon, 1972; Suthakar and Liberman, 2021) but also results in afferents fiber demyelination and ultimately loss of afferent fiber and their somas within the spiral ganglia over months to years (Kurioka et al., 2016; Nadol, 1997; Spoendlin, 1975; Webster and Webster, 1981).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Work focusing on changes in the vestibular periphery following hair cell loss has reported a similar reduction in vestibular afferent somas.
source: Likewise, work to date focusing on changes in the vestibular periphery following hair cell loss has reported a similar reduction in vestibular afferent somas (Ishiyama et al., 2004).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Electrical stimulation of auditory afferents via a cochlear prosthesis has been shown to protect auditory afferents from further degeneration.
source: However, promisingly for vestibular as well as cochlear implantation, electrical stimulation of auditory afferents via a cochlear prosthesis has been shown to protect auditory afferents from further degeneration (reviewed in Shibata et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: A recent study in monkeys found that vestibular implants can effectively evoke eye movements even when the prosthesis was implanted 10 years after bilateral labyrinthectomy.
source: Furthermore, a recent study in monkeys found that vestibular implants can effectively evoke eye movements, even when the prosthesis was implanted 10 years after bilateral labyrinthectomy, demonstrating that vestibular implants are likely to be effective even if some afferents have been lost (Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2023).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Nearly all vestibular prostheses have been designed to restore semicircular canal rather than otolith function.
source: To date, nearly all vestibular prostheses have been designed to restore semicircular canal rather than otolith function.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing current state of prosthesis development.

claim: Natural head movements generally comprise both rotational and linear motion, so inputs from both the semicircular canal and otolith are typically processed simultaneously and integrated for both behavior and perception.
source: However, since natural head movements generally comprises both rotational and linear motion, inputs from both the semicircular canal and otolith are typically processed simultaneously and integrated for both behavior and perception (reviewed in Angelaki and Cullen, 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Hair cells in the otolith organs are distributed over the neuroepithelia surface in a systematic manner that comprises a directional tuning map, with the axis of greatest sensitivity perpendicular to the curved line across the otolith organs.
source: A key feature of the otoliths is that their hair cells are distributed over the neuroepithelia surface in a systematic manner that comprises a directional tuning map, with the axis of greatest sensitivity perpendicular to the curved line across the otolith organs (Figure 11A, orange lines).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 11A, representing established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Stimulating the otoliths in a directionally specific manner requires a great number of electrodes that can selectively and independently stimulate a very focused area of the organ.
source: Consequently, stimulating the otoliths in a directionally specific manner requires a great number of electrodes that can selectively and independently stimulate a very focused area of the organ.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing an inference from anatomical knowledge applied to prosthesis design.

claim: The Della Santina laboratory has recently implanted a multichannel planar stimulating array in the otoliths of chinchillas.
source: Despite these challenges, the Della Santina laboratory has recently implanted a multichannel planar stimulating array in the otoliths of chinchillas (Figure 11A, gray circles).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 11A, representing recent experimental work.

claim: Stimulation of the otoliths using the implant successfully generated torsional and vertical eye movements consistent with vestibulo-ocular responses to tilt and translation.
source: Stimulation of the otoliths using the implant successfully generated torsional and vertical eye movements consistent with vestibulo-ocular responses to tilt and translation (Hageman et al., 2020), indicating successful stimulation of sections of the otolith sensitive to different axes of head motion.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Unlike pulsatile stimulation that can only evoke more firing in the targeted nerve, DC stimulation can both increase and decrease the firing.
source: Unlike pulsatile stimulation that can only evoke more firing in the targeted nerve (and thus requires baseline stimulation rate in order to encode motion in opposing directions), DC stimulation can both increase and decrease the firing.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing a comparison of stimulation approaches.

claim: Safe DC stimulation of the semicircular canals has been shown to evoke robust VOR eye movements consistent with the canal plane being stimulated in chinchillas.
source: In the context of the vestibular prosthesis, safe DC stimulation of the semicircular canals has been shown to evoke robust VOR eye movements consistent with the canal plane being stimulated in chinchillas (Aplin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Cathodic and anodic DC currents evoked eye movement in the excitatory and inhibitory (opposite) directions, respectively.
source: Specifically, cathodic and anodic currents evoked eye movement in the excitatory and inhibitory (opposite) directions, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing experimental findings.

claim: When compared to traditional pulsatile stimulation, DC stimulation provided a larger dynamic range of the evoked eye movements due to the ability to also inhibit activity.
source: Importantly, when compared to traditional pulsatile stimulation, DC stimulation provided a larger dynamic range of the evoked eye movements due to the ability to also inhibit activity.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text, representing a comparison of experimental findings.

claim: Electrophysiology and modeling studies have both shown that DC stimulator modulates afferent firing rate in a manner that also maintains their firing properties (irregularity and asynchronous behavior of firing).
source: Additionally, electrophysiology (Manca et al., 2019) and modeling (Steinhardt and Fridman, 2021) studies have both shown that DC stimulator modulates afferent firing rate in a manner that also maintains their firing properties (i.e. irregularity and asynchronous behavior of firing).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Recent studies quantifying afferent responses to transcranial DC stimulation of the vestibular system (galvanic vestibular stimulation) have shown that a transfer function between current delivered and afferent firing can be readily constructed and accounted for to evoke desired firing and head motion encoding within the afferents.
source: Fortunately, recent studies, quantifying afferent responses to transcranial DC stimulation of the vestibular system (i.e. galvanic vestibular stimulation), have shown that a transfer function between current delivered and afferent firing can be readily constructed and accounted for to evoke desired firing and head motion encoding within the afferents (Forbes et al., 2020; Forbes et al., 2023; Kwan et al., 2019; Figure 11C and D).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figures 11C and 11D, representing experimental findings from published research.

claim: Conventional mappings that did not account for high-pass dynamics of vestibular afferents resulted in decreasing gain and increasingly lagging phase of the evoked VOR.
source: Indeed, a recent study has confirmed the theoretical scenario above (Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022). Conventional mappings that did not account for high-pass dynamics of vestibular afferents resulted in decreasing gain and increasingly lagging phase of the evoked VOR, while biomimetic mappings that incorporated high-pass tuning resulted in more robust gain and more accurate phase of the evoked VOR (Figure 5, bottom; Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 5, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: Biomimetic mappings that incorporated high-pass tuning resulted in more robust gain and more accurate phase of the evoked VOR.
source: Indeed, a recent study has confirmed the theoretical scenario above (Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022). Conventional mappings that did not account for high-pass dynamics of vestibular afferents resulted in decreasing gain and increasingly lagging phase of the evoked VOR, while biomimetic mappings that incorporated high-pass tuning resulted in more robust gain and more accurate phase of the evoked VOR (Figure 5, bottom; Wiboonsaksakul et al., 2022).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation and illustrated in Figure 5, representing experimental data from published research.

claim: Mapping strategies biased toward the response dynamics of regular afferents yielded better VOR performance than a mapping strategy based on the response dynamics of irregular afferents.
source: Moreover, mapping strategies biased toward the response dynamics of regular afferents yielded better VOR performance than a mapping strategy based on the response dynamics of irregular afferents (Figure 10, blue and purple vs. red).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 10, representing experimental findings.

claim: This finding is consistent with prior experimental findings demonstrating that regular afferents make a more significant contribution to VOR pathway than do their irregular counterparts.
source: This finding is consistent with prior experimental findings demonstrating that regular afferents make a more significant contribution to VOR pathway than do their irregular counterparts (Boyle et al., 1992; Goldberg et al., 1987; Highstein et al., 1987; Minor and Goldberg, 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to published research.
